Three Biggest Ways to Fail Players in Free-to-Play Games

Only time will tell if it will continue to be successful and there are some initial teething problems but it looks like the early adopters have benefited so far.

Back-testing LTV models

Gaining lifetime users is hugely beneficial to mobile developers but in order to achieve this, we need to calculate the lifetime value of our users. With an array of models for calculating LTV, check out this back-testing guide to find the method right for you.

Piracy is a big problem for premium iPhone and iPad games — much more than you realize

In this report, William Volk has uncovered that 8 of the top 10 iOS games are available free of charge due to piracy. One contributing factor is the fact that users no longer need to jailbreak a game to download pirated games. In Volk’s opinion, premium games are no longer a viable option because of this widespread piracy.

Activision Blizzard to buy King for $5.9 billion

In what will be one of the biggest news stories of the year for the mobile game industry, King Digital Entertainment has been purchased by Activision Blizzard. The Candy Crush creatores will be bought out for $5.9 billion after a unanimous decision by the Activision Blizzard board. The deal is subject to approval from King shareholders and the Irish High Court.

Imagining what Google’s hybrid Android-plus-Chrome OS might look like

According to a recent report from The Wall Street Journal, Chrome OS and Android may soon be merged, with an official release happening in 2017. The focus of this combination is to expand the Andoird OS to laptops. An early version of this new OS is scheduled for preview sometime next year.

iOS 9 is now on 66% of Apple’s mobile devices

Apple announced this week that iOS 9 has now been adopted by the majority of Apple’s mobile devices. The new OS can now be found on two out of three Apple devices only two months after its initial launch. This is a huge improvement on the adoption of iOS 8 which only reached 52% of devices at the same stage of its release.

Conclusion: if you want to like it, you'll like it; if you want to hate it, you can quite effectively hate it. It's a alternate history scifi FPS adventure game, clearly drawing inspiration from System Shock 2. The game itself has a wonderful atmosphere and does several things very very well, but the action elements are... meh (there's actually an option to turn off combat and after about 20 mins I did that). The puzzles are pretty good, and the voice acting is better than expected for something this indie (ie, 2 people). One could consider the graphics either appropriately stylized or simply poor, I'm a forgiving person so I thought they were fine. The puzzles were pretty good actually, though I ended up looking something up because I am impatient and missed something. There are at least two endings and it is pretty clear which is 'good' and which is 'bad' (I got the bad one). My first run through took me about 3 hours, I could prob do it again in half that time. For fans of this type of game that want to like it I'd give it a 7.5, for everyone else a 6, for the cruel a 3 or 4, if you want to hate on the lackluster combat, questionable controls, simple graphics etc there's plenty to hate on. The sound employs some special mixing for headphones, though, that made it sound pretty damn good.

I've been enjoying it quite a bit for some reason; there are persistent elements that make me feel like I'm not wasting my time as well as rather difficult challenges to unlock new characters and traits and stuff. If you like weird unique roguelikes I give it an 8.5, regular people a 7, assholes a 5 or 6.

Deadnaut Another game from my Halloween budget gaming list, Deadnaut is the nichiest of niche games and defies quick and easy description but here's my attempt without describing the game systems very much: the player controls a team of expendable space explore in the far future, sending them in to investigate (randomly generated) derelict spaceships left behind by (randomly generated) extinct alien civilizations, where they will find (also randomly generated) threats they will need to overcome; each campaign is 4 ships long using the same aliens and threats. The graphics and sound are minimalist at best, and it plays kind of like the old Syndicate game or the more recent Satellite Reign. The game has a demo on Steam and if this sounds at all interesting I urge you to check it out, it actually got an update this week (!). I give it a 8.5 for me, 6.5 for average person, 4 or 5 for pricks.

Tormentum While playing MGSV I decided I wanted a short break from stealth action and opted for a mostly traditional point n click adventure that I bought one night drunk, played for an hour and got stuck. Tormentum is gorgeous, it has a beautifully garish and macabre art style that is very reminiscent of Giger, though it lacks the detail of Giger's work. Regardless, the art is excellent. The game, ehhhh, nothing special and if the art wasn't so good I doubt I'd have finished it (which only took 3.5 hours anyway). The puzzles are mostly simple, the hardest part is not mistaking something important for a bit of background. The writing is clearly translated from something else (Polish) and is occasionally awkward; personally I didn't mind this too much, I just pretended it was translated from demon speak or whatever the fuck, but GOOD writing would have been nice. There are some moral choices with pretty obvious good and bad options, I think you need to go all good to get the good ending, whatever, I went all bad cuz I'm fucking like that. An acceptable diversion with an extra point for the art (which really is excellent) and the dark subject matter, a generous 8.0 for me, 7 for the average joe, 5 for those with no appreciation for art. There's a demo.

Infinite Space 3: Sea of Stars I liked Infinite Space 2 quite a bit, it was a space exploration roguelike where you have a set amount of time to investigate as many planets as possible and collect as much stuff, upgrading your ship and gaining allies along the way. It took place on a 2D plane, was randomly generated, and was a nice thing to play while eating (ie, not really any action and only need the mouse). I threw in on the Early Access for part 3 over a year ago and it came out last month to, well, mixed reviews. Lots of people said it's shit so I didn't bother checking it out until last week when I suddenly remembered it for some reason. I dunno what people are complaining about, it's basically the same as IS2 but with a 3D map now (which is somewhat difficult to navigate, tbh). Maybe I haven't played it enough but it seems like the same amount of content. At 2 hrs played I'm giving it a 8 but that is tentative and subject to change, call it 7 for normies and 5 for dildos.

Sun Dogs Failbetter Games, the cool dudes behind the PC indie game Sunless Sea and the browser game Fallen London (both are aweome imo) suggested this on their Facebook page; I am not prone to joining or Liking things on FB but somehow this happened and I am glad it did because otherwise I'd probably have missed this. Sun Dogs is not much of a game, tbh; it's a text adventure with a graphical map, honestly, and even as a text adventure it's not very good: location descriptions seem to be generated semirandomly, as are 'quests' which are all seemingly simple fetch quests. It's really barely a game at all. What it IS is the first true, balls out transhuman/posthuman ANYTHING I've seen on PC since Too Human crashed and burned, and this is much more of the traditional scifi posthuman setting: humans wear bodies like clothing, are effectively immortal due to consciousness uploading, have expanded across the solar system, are linked to data networks and each other through bioimplants and nanotechnology, etc etc. It would be very familiar to anyone that has played the tabletop RPG Eclipse Phase. Anyway, the game is way overpriced at 10$ so I give it a generous 7.5 for me mostly for being the first to explore this setting on PC, a 5 for the average gamer, a 3 for asshats.

I'm gonna rapidfire the rest cause I didn't get far into them, I was just checking them out for later:

LISA Megadepressing but also very funny game with excellent writing, atypical characters, and surprisingly difficult traditional JRPG turnbased combat. I'll be coming back to this one.

Cards and Castles Decent CCG/boardgame mashup but real money booster packs turn me off.

Starship Traveller Fighting Fantasy Gamebook translated to PC (and probably mobile) game, decent if you know what you're in for but definitely an acquired taste and heavily reliant on luck.

Knock-Knock I dunno if I missed something or what but I spent 20 minutes just wandering around, turning on lights and reading 'cryptic' comments from the main character who looks a lot like someone I can't place but don't like. Maybe I'll return.

Neverending Nightmares A very arty mostly black and white hand drawn sidescrolling adventure game with waaaaay too much repetition. I get what they were going for but that doesn't make it fun. 45 mins was enough for me, I might come back if I read something compelling enough.

Steamalot: Epoch's Journey Pretty much the same fucking thing as Cards and Castles but no real money aspect, I'll give it a real shot someday.
Wasteland 2 and Divinity original sin for console. Super happy with these ports. Western turn based RPGs need more love!!!!
I'm waiting on these two to take a price drop ob Black Friday before I try to grab them.
